result:
The rain hit the glass not all at once but in waves, the way a thought arrives — half-formed, then suddenly the whole sentence. I stood there for twenty minutes without doing anything I would call productive. No phone. No book. Just the hiss of water tracing its way down the pane in long, impatient fingers.

What strikes me is how rare it is now to stand in front of something and let it be only itself. A puddle forms at the base of the window and simply sits there, gathering a small reflection of the streetlight above, undisturbed until the next wave of drops arrives and shatters it back into a thousand silver fragments. The light doesn't get angry about being broken. It just reassembles.

There's a particular loneliness in that. Not the loneliness of being alone in a crowd, which is more about noise and performance. This is a quieter thing — the loneliness of watching water do its only job, over and over, with no audience and no point. And being okay with it.

I think that's what I've been missing in recent years. The permission to be still in a way that isn't rest. Not the stillness of a phone set to do-not-disturb where the mind keeps drafting emails it will never send. This is the stillness of a puddle. It just receives. The rain falls, the glass holds it, the light makes it shine, and then the next drop comes and the pattern changes, and nothing was meant to be kept.

Twenty minutes. That was enough.
